results.summary: I checked every field of this section against the primary text and found no legal defect. The M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D definitions of 'sterile drug preparation' and 'complex non-sterile drug preparation', the three-limb definition of 'compounding' with its patient-specific significant-difference test, the express provision that a price difference shall not be a significant difference to justify compounding, and the closing 'except as provided in clause (1)' exclusion of commercially available federally approved drugs are all reproduced faithfully. The s. 39F(a) and (b) prohibitions, including the prescribe, ship, mail, sell, transfer and dispense verbs, and the s. 39F(c) cGMP-and-registration route and s. 39F(d) FDA-ban prohibition in ma_vs_federal, are accurate. The licence gates in 247 CMR 6.02(2) and (3) are stated correctly, including that 6.02(3) offers no institutional alternative. The 6.06(1) and 6.07(1) application items, the differing certified blueprints in 6.06(1)(b) and 6.07(1)(b), the satisfactory Board inspection ahead of issuance of the original licence in 6.06(2) and 6.07(2), the December 31 annual expiry in 6.06(3)(a) and 6.07(3)(a), and the renewal inspection-report submission in 6.06(3)(b) and 6.07(3)(b) all match the text. The section's hardest claims are its negative ones, and each verified: 247 CMR 6.15(2) does name only a sterile, non-resident sterile and institutional sterile compounding pharmacy; 6.15(4) does add a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy and does exclude a Drug Store pharmacy; 'replacing' is on the 6.15(2) list, so a like-for-like swap is inside it; four of the six 6.15(4) items are conditioned 'as applicable' or 'if applicable'; and no day count appears anywhere in 6.15. 247 CMR 9.01(3) reads exactly as quoted, and I confirmed that 247 CMR 9.00 contains no occurrence of 'hazardous' or 'engineering control', which supports the section's statement that the technical detail is not answered out of 247 CMR 9.00. The Board's own advisory 'USP <800> in Community Pharmacies' states that community pharmacies that only handle and dispense hazardous drugs in their final dosage form are still required to follow USP <800>, and lists receiving, storage, handling and dispensing, transportation and disposal, which supports the non-compounding overlay taught in orientation[6], comparison_tables[2] and worked_examples[3]. All eight listed practice questions (MA-Q-0214, MA-Q-0216, MA-Q-0217, MA-Q-0218, MA-Q-0219, MA-Q-0388, MA-Q-0435 and MA-Q-0436) are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it. Publishable to a candidate as it stands.

findings.location: orientation[7].text (first boundary, 'retention of the ordinary CQI file')
findings.problem: The section tells the candidate that the rules it teaches 'state a five-year period for serious-event records in 247 CMR 20.02(4) and state no period at all for a QRE record that never becomes reportable, so no such period is taught here and none should be inferred from the five-year figure.' Massachusetts does state one: 247 CMR 15.04(2) provides that each pharmacy shall maintain a record of all QREs for a minimum period of two years from the date of the QRE report.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 15.04 is titled 'Records' and sits in the same regulation, 247 CMR 15.00, whose 15.02 and 15.03 this section teaches in exhaustive detail; it is the subsection immediately after the last provision the section works through. The sentence is not a mere omission, it is an affirmative negative that forecloses the question and instructs the candidate not to look for a period. Record-retention intervals are among the most directly tested MPJE facts, so a candidate applying this section to Massachusetts facts would answer that no period is stated where the correct answer is two years from the date of the QRE report. 247 CMR 15.04 also requires a written copy of the CQI Program description to be kept on the pharmacy premises and readily available to all pharmacy personnel (15.04(1)), requires QRE records to be maintained in an orderly manner and filed by date (15.04(3)), and permits QRE records to be stored at a site other than the pharmacy where the QRE occurred (15.04(4)); none of that appears in the section either. The second boundary in the same paragraph, about confidentiality, is by contrast correct: I read the whole of 247 CMR 15.00 and it confers no confidentiality, privilege or discovery protection on a QRE record.

findings.location: timing_deadlines[] (no entry for QRE record retention) and forms_records[] (no entry for 247 CMR 15.04)
findings.problem: The timing_deadlines field carries the 24-hour QRE documentation clock, the annual CQI education interval, the designated indicator period, the two seven-business-day Board reports, the five-year serious-event retention and the 24-hour theft, loss or suspected tampering report, but no entry for the two-year QRE record retention in 247 CMR 15.04(2). With orientation[7] having told the candidate that no such period exists, the section contains no correct figure to fall back on.
findings.rationale: The section treats retention periods as timing material, since the five-year serious-event retention is itself a timing_deadlines entry and a common_traps entry. The QRE retention interval belongs in the same field. 247 CMR 15.04(2) fixes it at a minimum of two years measured from the date of the QRE report, which is also a different start point from the five-year period's 'date the report is filed with the Board' in 247 CMR 20.02(4), a contrast this section is otherwise well placed to teach.

findings.location: exceptions[] (no entry for 247 CMR 20.02(5)); comparison_tables[2].rows[0] ('Who reports'); orientation[4]; role_duties[8] and role_duties[9]
findings.problem: 247 CMR 20.02(5) provides that the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies. The section teaches 20.02(1) through (4) as duties of 'a Manager of Record of a pharmacy' and never states this express carve-out, although its exceptions field carries five other entries.
findings.rationale: The section's declared subtopic is 'the seven-business-day serious-event reports and five-year records in 247 CMR 20.02', and 20.02(5) is a subsection of that very provision which limits the reach of everything the section teaches from it. The gap is not academic: 247 CMR 20.07(3) gives a non-resident pharmacy a parallel but materially different duty, to report improper dispensing into Massachusetts that results in serious injury or death 'within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing', where 20.02(1) runs from discovery of the serious injury or death. The section repeatedly and correctly drills the candidate that the 20.02(1) clock does not start at the dispensing (orientation[4], worked_examples[0] step 4, common_traps), so a candidate carrying that rule onto non-resident facts would reach the wrong start date under a provision the section never signals exists.

findings.location: decision_logic[7].action (condition: 'Controlled substances are missing, or a container or shipment shows signs of interference')
findings.problem: The action directs the candidate to report to the Drug Control Program within the Department on its form 'rather than to the Board'. On a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances Massachusetts also requires a Board report: 247 CMR 20.03(7) obliges a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy and nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to submit to the Board a copy of the 'Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance' and DEA Form 106 within seven days.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 700.008 itself says nothing about the Board, so 'rather than to the Board' is the section's own inference rather than the regulation's words, and as a general proposition about Massachusetts theft and loss reporting it is wrong. The section's prose gets this right everywhere else by using the precise formulation that a report to the Board 'does not answer this regulation' (orientation[6], worked_examples[2] step 3). The condition of this decision_logic entry is broader than suspected tampering: it opens with 'Controlled substances are missing', which is exactly the significant-loss case 247 CMR 20.03(7) reaches, so a candidate taught to route a discovered loss away from the Board would omit a required Massachusetts report. Because the omitted report is a state one, the section's separate and correct note that the federal theft-or-loss route is taught elsewhere does not cover it.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 247 CMR 20.03(7) (theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances reported to the Board)

results.summary: The teaching in this section is accurate wherever it paraphrases a provision, and I verified it line by line. 247 CMR 15.02(1)(a)-(f), the four purpose verbs and all six minimum provisions; 247 CMR 15.03(1)(a)-(c), including that the professional-judgment qualifier attaches to the prescriber notification alone; 247 CMR 15.03(2)(a)'s 24-hour clock and 15.03(2)(b)1.-4.'s four content elements; 247 CMR 15.03(3)(a)1.-3. and 15.03(3)(b)'s response half; 247 CMR 20.02(1)-(4), including the three recipients, the two different clock starts and the five-year readily retrievable retention measured from filing; and 105 CMR 700.008 word for word, are all correct. All nine listed practice questions (MA-Q-0051, MA-Q-0052, MA-Q-0053, MA-Q-0055, MA-Q-0056, MA-Q-0057, MA-Q-0089, MA-Q-0115 and MA-Q-0369) are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it. Three defects keep it from KEEP. The serious one is orientation[7], which tells the candidate that no retention period exists for a QRE record that never becomes reportable and that none should be inferred; 247 CMR 15.04(2) requires QRE records to be kept a minimum of two years from the date of the QRE report, and that figure appears nowhere in the section's timing material. Second, 247 CMR 20.02(5) expressly excludes non-resident pharmacies from the whole of 247 CMR 20.02 and the section teaches 20.02 without it, while 247 CMR 20.07(3) gives non-resident pharmacies a different start point, discovery of the improper dispensing, that inverts the very trap the section drills. Third, decision_logic[7] routes a discovered controlled-substance loss to the Drug Control Program 'rather than to the Board', when 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Board report with DEA Form 106 within seven days for a theft or loss of a significant amount. All three are correctable in place: one paragraph in orientation, one added timing and records entry, one added exceptions entry with a qualification to the 20.02 actor rows, and one decision_logic action re-worded. The section's structure, tables, worked examples and retrieval prompts otherwise stand.
